title: Synthesis --- The Choices English Never Makes You Make

lessons.title: Synthesis — the choices English never makes you make
lessons.gloss: synthesis — three places where English hands you one word and Spanish makes you choose

segments.text: Nothing new here. Two verbs to say aloud first: traer, conocer.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one English word, two Spanish verbs

segments.text: Three times now you have met a pair of verbs where English makes do with one. They arrived chapters apart and have never been put side by side:

utterances: English gives you: to ask. Spanish makes you choose: preguntar, pedir. the question you must answer: asking a question, or asking for a thing?
English gives you: to bring / take. Spanish makes you choose: traer, llevar. the question you must answer: toward the speaker, or away?
English gives you: to know. Spanish makes you choose: conocer, saber. the question you must answer: a person or place, or a fact?

segments.text: None of these is a vocabulary problem. In each one, the word is easy and the decision is the work — and the decision is information English speakers are simply never required to supply.

When you pick traer over llevar, you have told your listener where you are standing. When you pick conocer over saber, you have told them whether you have met the thing or only heard of it. The grammar is carrying meaning that English would need a whole clause to add.
You are not translating any more. You are choosing.
— ¿Conoces Madrid? — Sí, conozco Madrid. Pero no sé dónde está el café.
Two "knows" in two lines, and not interchangeable. The first is acquaintance — I have been there. The second is a fact. English uses know for both and loses the difference.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the exchange above, both parts]

segments.text: Until the choice happens before you notice making it.

segments.prompt: You want to say you know a person. Conocer or saber?

feedback.correct: Yes — conocer is for people and places you have met.

segments.prompt: Someone asks you to move something toward where they are. Traer or llevar?

feedback.correct: Yes — traer moves it toward the speaker.

segments.prompt: You want to ask for a coffee, not ask a question. Preguntar or pedir?

feedback.correct: Yes — pedir is asking FOR something.
feedback.incorrect: Pedir. Preguntar is asking a question.

segments.text: What does choosing traer tell your listener? (Where you are standing.) What does choosing conocer tell them? (That you have met it, not just heard of it.) And which of the three pairs did you learn first? (Preguntar and pedir — long before the other two.)
